UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Maryland Office of People’s Counsel                               )
                                                                  )
          v.                                                      ) Docket No. EL26-63-000
                                                                  )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                       )
and Transmission Owners Designated Under Attachment A             )
to the Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement                 )
(CTOA)                                                            )



               ANSWER OF OLD DOMINION ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE
                        IN OPPOSITION TO COMPLAINT

    I.   INTRODUCTION

         Pursuant to Rules 206(f) and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18

C.F.R. §§ 385.206(f), 385.213 (2025), and the Commission’s Notice of Amended Complaint and

Extension of Time,1 Old Dominion Electric Cooperative (“ODEC”) submits this answer in

opposition to the Amended Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing of the Maryland Office

of People’s Counsel (May 22, 2026) (“Complaint”). The Complaint contends that because of the

development of large data center loads in some zones within the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”) region, Maryland ratepayers are unfairly subsidizing those data center loads with respect

to the cost allocation for baseline Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) projects that

are necessitated by the large data center loads. The Complaint requests immediate, fast-track relief

for cost allocation of baseline reliability RTEP projects related to large loads, including that the

Commission (1) find that the cost allocation provisions in Schedule 12 of PJM’s Open Access

1
 Maryland Office of the People’s Counsel v. AEP Transmission Co, Inc., Docket No. EL26-63-000 (May
22, 2026).
 Transmission Tariff (“OATT” or “Tariff”) are unjust and unreasonable as applied to baseline

RTEP reliability upgrade costs driven by large load growth; (2) establish a refund effective date

no later than 60 days after the date of the Complaint filing; (3) direct PJM to re-study baseline

reliability projects approved in last three RTEP procurement windows to determine the extent to

which transmission system impacts and costs were caused by expected load growth from data

centers versus other causes and allocate those costs to the zone where the data center load is or

will be located; and (4) direct PJM to develop and submit to the Commission a revised cost

allocation methodology for RTEP baseline reliability costs that assigns transmission costs

associated with large load interconnections to the zones where those large loads are located, with

credits back to transmission zones that previously collected those costs. The Complaint also

requests that the Commission direct PJM to undertake a redesign of its planning, interconnection

and cost allocation processes for large loads conditioned on or in parallel with the ANOPR in

Docket No. RM26-4-000.2

          The Commission should reject the Complaint because it does not establish a prima facie

case that PJM’s Schedule 12 cost allocation for baseline RTEP reliability upgrade costs driven by

large load growth is unjust and unreasonable. Further, even if the Commission were to determine

that the Complaint meets the statutory requirements and the Commission’s regulations, which it

does not, the Commission should reject the Complaint as moot since subsequent to the Complaint,

the Commission initiated a proceeding under FPA section 206 to address the issues raised in the

Complaint.3


2
  Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Advance Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 23, 2025) (“ANOPR”); Interconnection of Large Loads to the
Interstate Transmission System, Notice Inviting Comments, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025)
(inviting comments on the Secretary of Energy’s proposed ANOPR).
3
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 (June 18, 2026) (“Show Cause Order”).
           ODEC is not only a PJM Transmission Owner, but also a load-serving entity (“LSE”) for

its eleven electric distribution cooperative members located in Virginia, Maryland and Delaware.

As such, ODEC has been significantly impacted by the challenges presented by integration of large

loads, including cost allocation. ODEC opposes the Complaint for the reasons discussed herein.

However, ODEC also supports efforts by PJM, the PJM Transmission Owners and the

Commission, among others, to ensure that the costs associated with accommodating large loads

are borne by the new large loads driving them. This cost allocation principle should apply

consistently to both PJM Supplemental Projects and Baseline RTEP projects. 4 ODEC also

reiterates that the Commission must ensure that reliability remains uncompromised as these

unprecedented loads are integrated.

    II.   DISCUSSION

              A. The Commission Should Reject the Complaint for Failing to Satisfy FPA

                  Section 206 and the Commission’s Regulations.

          Under FPA section 206, complainants must demonstrate that the existing rate, charge,

classification, rule, regulation, practice or contracts at issue are unjust, unreasonable, unduly

discriminatory or preferential.5 Additionally, the Commission’s regulations require that

complaints “[c]learly identify the action or inaction which is alleged to violate applicable statutory

standards or regulatory requirements”6 and “[e]xplain how the action or inaction violates

applicable statutory standards or regulatory requirements.”7 The Commission has explained that



4
 See ODEC Comments filed in Docket No. RM26-4-000 on November 21, 2025, at 9 (ELibrary Accession
No. 20251121-5343).
5
    16 U.S.C. § 824e(b); see, e.g., FirstEnergy Serv. Co. v. FERC, 758 F.3d 346, 353 (D.C. Cir. 2014).
6
    18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(1) (2025).
7
    18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(2).
 in order to meet this burden of proof and the Commission’s regulations, complaints must provide

specific evidence and analysis, as opposed to unsupported conclusions.

           The Complaint contends that “PJM’s hybrid cost allocation methodology produces unjust

and unreasonable rates for Maryland customers because it requires them to pay for regional

transmission projects driven primarily by concentrated data center load growth.”8 According to the

Complaint, PJM’s existing cost allocation for baseline RTEP projects caused by large data centers

is unjust and unreasonable because (1) the load-ratio share component of PJM’s hybrid cost

allocation methodology does not reflect the geographic concentration of load growth that causes

the costs; and (2) on a technical basis, the solution-based DFAX component of PJM’s baseline

RTEP cost allocation is not suited for cost allocation for projects necessitated by data center

reliability. The Complaint further argues that even if the solution-based DFAX were technically

appropriate, speculative load forecasts and “phantom” requests render DFAX allocations arbitrary.

These broad claims are supported only by generalized, conclusory assertions as opposed to specific

evidence and analysis. This is insufficient to establish a prima facie case that the entirety of the

cost allocation provisions in Schedule 12 of the PJM Tariff are unjust and unreasonable as applied

to assignment of RTEP baseline reliability upgrade costs driven by large load growth.

           The Complaint relies on the fact that based on the three most recent RTEP windows,

approximately $1.6 billion in transmission costs will be allocated to Maryland over the next ten

(10) years.9 The Complaint then concludes that because the overwhelming majority of these costs

are for transmission necessitated by large loads and Maryland’s load growth does not match this




8
    Complaint at 29.
9
    Id. at 6, Table 2.
 rate of transmission development, PJM’s Schedule 12 cost allocation is unjust and unreasonable.10

The lack of specificity in providing evidence that the PJM Tariff provisions for cost allocation are

resulting in unjust and unreasonable rates, particularly for Maryland ratepayers, is insufficient to

satisfy the Commission’s requirements that complaints must “[c]learly identify the action or

inaction which is alleged to violate applicable statutory standards or regulatory requirements”11

and “[e]xplain how the action or inaction violates applicable statutory standards or regulatory

requirements.”12 The Complaint makes several conclusory and conditional assertions but does not

provide analysis, such as identification and analysis of specific RTEP baseline reliability projects,

to demonstrate that the increase in RTEP costs allocated to Maryland is not “roughly

commensurate” with benefits received.13 Instead, the Complaint simply asserts that Maryland

ratepayers do not “meaningfully benefit” from these facilities.14

           ODEC fully acknowledges that large loads, predominantly data centers, are the primary

driver of the unprecedented growth in electricity demand, and that this growth is expected to


10
   Complaint at 20-23; see also Affidavit of Ron Nelson and Andy Eiden, Attachment A to Complaint, at
62 (claiming that there is a “dramatic gap” between the costs assigned to Maryland through PJM’s current
cost allocation methods and the level of load growth occurring in Maryland” and, therefore, “PJM’s cost
allocation 10 methodology results in an unjust and unreasonable outcome for Maryland 11 ratepayers.”)
11
     18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(1) (2025).
12
   18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(2). See, e.g., Champion Energy Marketing LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
and PJM Settlement, Inc., 153 FERC ¶ 61,059 at PP 29-30 (2015) (The Commission rejected a complaint
challenging that the operation and application of PJM’s Tariff provisions regarding Balancing Operating
Reserve charges was unjust and unreasonable, where the complainant relied on the fact that it was assessed
a large amount of such charges. In rejecting the Complaint the Commission stated, in part, that the fact that
charges were high “does not demonstrate that the applicable PJM Tariff provisions are unjust or
unreasonable” since PJM took actions to maintain reliability that benefits all load, including the
complainant.)
13
   The Complaint and attached Affidavit broadly contend that the 2022 RTEP Window 3 “may have included costs
related to short circuits” and points to a Reactive Power VAR Reinforcement as evidence that the solution-based
DFAX cost allocation is not just and reasonable as applied to transmission projects necessitated by large loads.
Complaint at 39. These two references, which are uncertain from complainants’ perspective, are insufficient to
demonstrate that the existing cost allocation is unjust and unreasonable for the entire category of baseline RTEP
transmission projects that are “caused” by data center large loads.
14
     Complaint at 68.
 continue. ODEC also recognizes that PJM’s RTEP includes unprecedented amounts of

transmission facilities in order to maintain reliability of the transmission system as necessary to

serve large loads. Indeed, the Commission has taken action in numerous proceedings to address

the challenges associated with integrating large loads into the transmission system in a timely,

efficient and reliable manner, including cost allocation.15 However, the pressing nature of these

issues does not excuse the Complaint’s failure to satisfy the statutory and regulatory requirements

to provide sufficient support. Therefore, the Commission should reject the Complaint.

          Additionally, ODEC emphasizes its disagreement with the replacement rate suggested in

the Complaint. Among other things, the Complaint requests that the Commission direct PJM to

allocate the costs of baseline transmission projects driven by data centers directly to the zones in

which they are or will be located.16 There is no demonstration that such a blanket directive would

result in rates that are just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Quite to the

contrary, simply dumping the costs for transmission projects necessitated by data centers on all

customers in the zone where the data centers are located, will simply create a new cost allocation

that would likely be unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory and preferential. There is zero

evidence that in every instance, all load in the zone will benefit from all baseline RTEP

transmission projects necessitated by data centers, even on a roughly commensurate basis. As a

load-serving entity in Virginia that is already bearing costs for facilities necessitated by large loads

that ODEC neither caused nor receives commensurate benefits, ODEC has critical concerns over

attempts to throw costs off to zones where data centers are located. The Commission should reject




15
     See Show Cause Order at PP 11-18.
16
     See Complaint at 69.
 the Maryland OPC’s suggestion to adopt an unreasonable cost allocation methodology.17 Instead,

as discussed immediately below, the Commission should dismiss the Complaint and continue to

address the issues in the Show Cause Order.

                  B. The Commission Should Dismiss the Complaint as Moot

           For the reasons discussed above, the Commission should reject the Complaint for failing

to satisfy FPA section 206 and the Commission’s implementing regulations. However, even if the

Commission does not reject the Complaint, it should dismiss the Complaint as moot because the

issues raised in the Complaint are pending in the Show Cause Order.

           The Complaint states that there are no pending proceedings at the Commission or in any

other forum that address the specific cost challenges raised in the Complaint.18 Of course, at the

time the Complaint was filed, the DOE ANOPR was pending before the Commission. Indeed, the

Complaint relies on the DOE ANOPR as confirmation that the remedy proposed in the Complaint

is a “logical extension of existing Commission policy to a class of grid participants that now

impose system impacts comparable to generators.”19 Thus, Complainants seem to recognize that

the DOE ANOPR at least addresses issues raised in the Complaint to some extent. The DOE

ANOPR remains pending before the Commission.

           Moreover, subsequent to the submission of the Complaint, the Commission issued the

Show Cause Order. There, the Commission instituted its own FPA section 206 proceeding and



17
   See FirstEnergy Solutions Corp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 143 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 44 (2013) (In
rejecting the complaint, the Commission determined that the complainant was essentially “arguing that the
current allocation . .. be replaced with an equally, if not more, arbitrary mechanism. While some parties,
like [complainant], may benefit from sch a reallocation, [complainant] has not shown that such a
reallocation will benefit the overall market structure in PJM nor allocate costs to those that cause the costs
to be incurred or have the incentive to reduce those costs.”).
18
     Complaint at 72.
19
     Id. at 65.
 directed PJM and the PJM TOs, including ODEC, to demonstrate that the Tariff remains just and

reasonable without provisions that address (1) application process, study procedures and ongoing

operational requirements regarding transmission service for large loads; (2) transparency regarding

Network Upgrade costs to provide transmission service for large loads, “a pro forma cost recovery

agreement between PJM, the relevant transmission owner and Eligible Customer taking

transmission service on behalf of the large load to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among

transmission customers, and a mechanism to ensure such payments are appropriately credited

towards transmission owners’ transmission revenue requirements;” (3) transmission services that

reflect flexible large loads; and (4) rates, terms and conditions of service for interconnection

customers serving large load or co-located load.20 Alternatively, the Commission directed PJM

and the PJM Transmission Owners to explain what Tariff changes would remedy these concerns

if the Commission determines the Tariff is unjust and unreasonable, or submit filings under FPA

section 205 to address these issues.21 The Commission also directed PJM to submit an

informational report detailing how PJM will ensure generation resource adequacy with respect to

large loads.22 The Show Cause Order includes several questions for briefing and provides an

opportunity for interested entities to respond to PJM’s and the PJM Transmission Owners’ filings,

addressing whether the Tariff remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or

preferential, and/or if not, what changes to the Tariff should be implemented as a replacement

rate.23




20
     Show Cause Order at P 35 (emphasis added).
21

23

        The issues raised in the Complaint are at issue in the Show Cause Order and the

Commission should dismiss the Complaint as moot. The Show Cause Order includes a preliminary

determination that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable absent provisions that address, among

other things, an agreement that will include the large load customer and address cost allocation for

transmission projects necessary to serve large loads in order to mitigate the risk of cost shifting

and provide a mechanism to credit payments from the large loads for such transmission facilities

against the Transmission Owners’ transmission revenue requirements. The Show Cause Order not

only requires PJM and the Transmission Owners to address these issues, but it also provides an

opportunity for interested entities such as Maryland OPC to address the issues as well, in response

to PJM and/or the PJM TOs’ responses to the Show Cause Order. Having the issues addressed in

the Show Cause Order also promotes administrative efficiency and saves entities and the

Commission from needlessly spending resources on two proceedings that will address the same

issues. Given the breadth of the Show Cause Order and the Commission’s requirement that PJM

and all of the Transmission Owners respond, in addition to the Commission’s assurances that it

will take action on these matters on its own initiative if necessary, the Show Cause Order will

result in a more complete record than this proceeding for the Commission to make its decision.

       Further, addressing these matters in the Show Cause Order, as opposed to simultaneously

in both proceedings, is consistent with the Commission’s statutory authority. As the Commission

is the entity with the authority to determine the replacement rate under FPA section 206, not the

complainant in this proceeding, the Commission’s Show Cause proceeding is the appropriate

proceeding to determine what, if any, Tariff revisions are necessary. ODEC emphasizes here that

it is not predetermining that any changes should be required, and ODEC notes that PJM and/or the

Transmission Owners might opt to submit their own FPA section 205 filing(s) to address issues
 raised in the Show Cause Order. Regardless, the Commission should find that the Complaint has

been rendered moot by the Show Cause Order and, therefore, dismiss the Complaint.24 At the very

least, the Commission should hold the Complaint in abeyance and make it subject to the outcome

of the Show Cause proceeding.

III.    CONCLUSION

        WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, ODEC requests that the Commission reject the

Complaint in its entirety.
